messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 73

# Marcus

Marcus is a fifty-year-old plumber who has spent the last three decades building a reputation for reliability and craftsmanship in his community. He and his wife, Patricia, have been married for twenty-two years and live in the same neighborhood where he grew up. He takes pride in his work—the kind of pride that comes from doing something well and having people trust you to do it. Until eighteen months ago, his life followed a predictable rhythm: early mornings, honest labor, coming home to Patricia, weekends spent on small projects around the house.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in February. Marcus had been called to an emergency job at a commercial building downtown—a burst pipe in the basement that needed immediate attention. He arrived around seven o'clock, when the building was mostly empty. A man confronted him in the stairwell, demanded his wallet and tools. Marcus, who has never been one to back down, refused. What followed was violent and sudden. The man beat him with a crowbar, fracturing two ribs and leaving him with a concussion and deep lacerations across his back and shoulders. Marcus spent three nights in the hospital.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The rest did not.

Now, eighteen months later, Marcus moves through his days like someone perpetually braced for impact. Patricia notices that he no longer goes to jobs alone—he insists on bringing his apprentice, even when it's inefficient or costs him money. He checks and rechecks the locks on their doors multiple times each evening, sometimes getting out of bed at two in the morning to verify they're secure. Patricia has learned not to touch him unexpectedly; the startle response is violent and frightening for them both.

Work, which once grounded him, has become a minefield. He still takes plumbing jobs, but certain situations trigger an almost unbearable anxiety. Basement work makes his chest tight and his breathing shallow. Enclosed spaces feel suffocating. When he's in someone's home and they move suddenly in his peripheral vision, his body floods with adrenaline—his hands shake, sweat beads on his forehead, and he has to excuse himself to the bathroom to regain composure. He's turned down jobs, something he never did before, and his income has suffered. More painful than the financial impact is the erosion of his identity. He's always been the man people called when they needed something fixed. Now he's the man who can't handle a basement job.

Sleep is fragmented and unreliable. He lies awake replaying the assault—the sound of the crowbar, the smell of his own blood, the feeling of helplessness. When he does sleep, he dreams of being trapped, unable to move or call out. He wakes gasping, sometimes finding himself on the floor, uncertain how he got there.

What troubles Marcus most is the anger. It comes in waves, disproportionate and terrifying. Patricia mentioned once that she was thinking of taking a different route home from work, and Marcus erupted—not at her, but the rage was there, raw and consuming. He apologized immediately, but the look on her face told him she was frightened. He frightens himself. This isn't who he is. He's always been steady, dependable, calm. Now he feels like a stranger in his own skin, reactive and volatile, trapped in a body that won't let him forget what happened on that Tuesday in February.

He sits in the therapy office with his shoulders slightly hunched, hands folded tightly in his lap, waiting for someone to help him find his way back to himself.
